title: Which jobs need a high risk work licence in Australia?
description: The 29 high risk work licence classes in Schedule 3 of the model WHS Regulations, 5 year licence terms, training and assessment rules, and employer duties.
shortAnswer: Under the model Work Health and Safety Regulations used in every Australian jurisdiction except Victoria, a person must hold a high risk work licence to carry out any of the 29 classes of high risk work in Schedule 3, covering scaffolding, dogging and rigging, cranes and hoists, reach stackers, forklifts, boilers, steam turbines and reciprocating steam engines. Applicants must be at least 18, complete the specified VET course, and licences expire after 5 years.
keyTakeaways: Regulation 81 prohibits carrying out a class of high risk work without the matching licence. Schedule 3 lists 29 classes, and Schedule 4 sets the VET course required for each.
A licence lasts 5 years under regulation 92. Renewal requires a declaration that the holder has maintained competency, and the regulator may direct a reassessment if it doubts competence.
Trainees may do high risk work without a licence only while training towards certification and under the supervision of a licence holder, and the business must ensure direct supervision.
A business must see written evidence of a worker's licence before directing or allowing the work, and keep that record for at least 1 year.

In New South Wales, SafeWork NSW requires training with a registered training organization and assessment by a SafeWork NSW accredited assessor, and lapsed licences can be renewed for up to 12 months after expiry.
jurisdiction: Australia (model WHS laws; New South Wales example)
regulator: State and territory WHS regulators applying the model Work Health and Safety Regulations developed by Safe Work Australia, for example SafeWork NSW
appliesTo: Workers who erect scaffolding, perform dogging or rigging, or operate cranes, hoists, elevating work platforms, concrete placing booms, reach stackers or forklifts
Operators of boilers, steam turbines of 500 kW or more, and reciprocating steam engines with a piston diameter over 250 mm, common in power generation and processing plants
Persons conducting a business or undertaking (PCBUs) that direct or allow workers to carry out or supervise high risk work
Registered training organizations and accredited assessors delivering licence training and assessment

sections.heading: Where in Australia do the high risk work licence rules apply?

blocks.text: The licensing scheme comes from Part 4.5 of the [model Work Health and Safety Regulations](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-12/model-whs-regulations-5_december_2025.pdf) published by Safe Work Australia, which each jurisdiction adopts through its own regulation. According to Safe Work Australia's [history of the model WHS laws](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/law-and-regulation/history-model-whs-laws), Victoria is the only jurisdiction that has not implemented them, so the regulation numbers on this page apply in the Commonwealth, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory.

The licence requirement sits alongside the general duty in the WHS Act to provide information, training and instruction, covered in [the WHS Act duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training). A licence proves the worker passed a nationally specified course and assessment. It does not replace site specific induction or training on the plant actually in use.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the model WHS Regulations as published by Safe Work Australia on December 5, 2025 and SafeWork NSW guidance, as at November 2026. Each jurisdiction's own regulation is the law that applies, and fees, application steps and penalty amounts differ. Check the relevant regulator before relying on any detail.

sections.heading: What are the 29 classes of high risk work?

blocks.text: Schedule 3 of the model Regulations sets out 29 licence classes in six groups. Several crane and hoist classes require the dogging licence as well, under the VET course combinations in Schedule 4.

Tower crane; self-erecting tower crane; derrick crane; portal boom crane; bridge and gantry crane; vehicle loading crane of 10 metre tonnes or more; non-slewing mobile crane over 3 tonnes; slewing mobile cranes up to 20, 60 and 100 tonnes and over 100 tonnes; materials hoist; personnel and materials hoist; boom-type elevating work platform with a boom of 11 metres or more; concrete placing boom
Reach stacker over 3 tonnes capacity with a container lifting attachment
Standard boiler; advanced boiler; steam turbine with output of 500 kW or more meeting specified criteria; reciprocating steam engine with any piston diameter over 250 mm

blocks.text: The pressure equipment classes are the ones energy and processing businesses most often overlook. A steam turbine is in scope if it produces 500 kW or more and is multi-wheeled, can exceed 3,600 revolutions per minute, has attached condensers, or uses a multi-staged heat exchange extraction process.

sections.heading: What training and assessment is needed to get a licence?

blocks.text: Only a person who holds the qualification set out in Schedule 4 for a class may apply for that licence, under regulation 86. Each class maps to one or more specified VET courses, such as "Licence to perform dogging" plus "Licence to operate a tower crane" for the tower crane class. The application must include a certification for the VET course issued not more than 60 days earlier.

Under regulation 89 the regulator must be satisfied that the applicant is at least 18 years of age, has provided the certification, and is able to carry out the work safely and competently. In New South Wales, [SafeWork NSW](https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/licences-and-registrations/licences/high-risk-work-licences) adds that the applicant must have been trained by a registered training organization, assessed as competent by a SafeWork NSW accredited assessor working for that organization under realistic workplace conditions, and be able to speak English well enough to carry out the work safely with other people.

SafeWork NSW describes a three step process: apply online for an assessment enrolment number, complete the assessment with the accredited assessor, then apply for the licence within 60 days of the Notice of Satisfactory Assessment. The training provider side of this is governed by the [Standards for RTOs 2025](/regulations/standards-for-rtos-2025-training-and-assessment).

sections.heading: How long does a high risk work licence last, and how is it renewed?

blocks.text: A licence takes effect on the day it is granted and expires 5 years later, unless cancelled earlier, under regulation 92. Renewal under regulations 100 and 101 must be applied for before expiry and requires a declaration that the holder has maintained competency, including by obtaining any reassessment the regulator directed.

Regulation 95 lets the regulator direct a licence holder to obtain a reassessment of competency if it reasonably believes the holder may not be competent. The examples given are training or assessment that did not meet the required standard, and information that the holder has carried out high risk work incompetently.

SafeWork NSW applies these rules with some practical detail. Classes added later expire with the original licence, reminders are sent about 60 days before expiry, and a licence can be renewed up to 12 months after expiry. After that, the person must retrain with a registered training organization, be reassessed and apply again.

sections.heading: What must employers and site operators check?

blocks.text: A PCBU must not direct or allow a worker to carry out high risk work unless it has seen written evidence that the worker holds the relevant licence, under regulation 85(1). It must also see evidence of enrollment in training before allowing a trainee to do the work under supervision, and evidence that any supervisor holds the licence for that work.

Regulation 85(4) requires the PCBU to keep a record of the written evidence for at least 1 year after the high risk work is carried out, or for supervisors, 1 year after the last occasion on which they supervise. Regulation 84 requires direct supervision of trainees, meaning oversight that directs, demonstrates, monitors and checks the work at the trainee's level of competency and ensures capacity to respond in an emergency, unless direct supervision is impracticable or unnecessary and the reduced level will not create a risk.

blocks.text: The last row matters because a licence is portable across sites and jurisdictions, recognized under regulation 83, while the hazards are local. A [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) on the specific plant closes that gap. The guide on [building a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) shows how to track licence expiry alongside site training.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records each licence class as an external credential attached to a role, then links the role to the site specific knowledge and observation points the licence does not cover, such as the particular crane configuration or boiler control system. Licence expiry and site retraining can then be tracked against the same framework. See how this applies to [energy and resources organizations](/industries/energy-resources).

faqs.q: Is a high risk work licence from one state valid in another?
faqs.a: Yes, within the jurisdictions that use the model laws. Regulation 83 treats an equivalent licence granted under a corresponding WHS law as a high risk work licence, provided it is used in line with its conditions and is not suspended, cancelled or expired in the jurisdiction that granted it. Victoria has not implemented the model laws, so its licensing rules must be checked separately.

faqs.q: Does a telehandler need a forklift licence?
faqs.a: SafeWork NSW says a high risk work licence is not required for a telehandler fitted with forks or a bucket. The business still has a duty of care to ensure workers have appropriate training to operate a telehandler, so a documented training and competency check for the specific machine remains necessary.

faqs.q: Can someone operate a crane without a licence while setting it up?
faqs.a: Regulation 82(4) says a person setting up or dismantling a crane or hoist does not need a crane operator licence if they hold a rigging licence that qualifies them for the work. Separately, plant operated without a load solely for maintenance, testing or commissioning at the workplace is exempt under regulation 82(2).

faqs.q: Can a worker start high risk work as soon as they pass the assessment?
faqs.a: Under regulation 82(1A), a person holding certification for the specified VET course may do the work for 60 days after the certification is issued, and longer if they apply for the licence within that period, until the licence is granted or 28 days after notice of a refusal. SafeWork NSW lets workers present the Notice of Satisfactory Assessment while waiting.

factCheck.claim: Regulation 81 of the model WHS Regulations prohibits carrying out a class of high risk work without the relevant licence; Schedule 3 Table 3.1 lists 29 classes
Regulation 92 provides that a high risk work licence expires 5 years after the day it is granted unless cancelled earlier

Regulation 89 requires the applicant to be at least 18 years of age; regulation 87 requires certification issued not more than 60 days before application; regulation 86 limits applicants to holders of Schedule 4 qualifications
Regulation 85 requires a PCBU to see written evidence of the licence and keep the record for at least 1 year; regulation 84 requires direct supervision of trainees
Regulation 95 allows the regulator to direct reassessment of competency; regulation 101 requires a renewal declaration of maintained competency, made before expiry

Schedule 3 item 28 covers steam turbines of 500 kW or more that are multi-wheeled, exceed 3600 rpm, have attached condensers or multi-staged heat exchange extraction; item 29 covers reciprocating steam engines with a piston diameter over 250 mm
